newsitem.title: USA: USDA likely to raise sugar import quota - analysts.
newsitem.headline: USDA likely to raise sugar import quota - analysts.

text.p: The U.S. Agriculture Department was expected to increase the sugar import quota by 200,000 tonnes on Monday in the final use this year of a formula that assesses import needs, analysts said Friday.
"This (increase) would appear to us to be pretty automatic," said Tom Hammer, president of Sweetener Users Association, a trade group for bakers and drink makers.
An American Sugar Alliance analyst said it might be a close call but it was more likely the increase would be approved.
Under the USDA formula, the quota goes up 200,000 tonnes if the projected stocks-to-use ratio is 15.5 percent or less.
In April, USDA forecast a ratio of 14.4 percent, compared to 14 percent in March, when a 200,000-tonne increase was approved. The ratio was too high in January for an increase.

Even with an increase in the quota this month, the Sweetener Users Association said in a letter to Agriculture Secretary Dan Glickman "you may be called upon to use your discretionary authority to increase the FY97 sugar import quota."

For fiscal 1997, USDA said it would use the stocks-to-use ratio to decide in January, March and May whether to allow more sugar into the country above the 1.7 million tonnes allocated at the start of the fiscal year.
Review dates were the same as release dates for the monthly World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates report. The May issue will be released Monday at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT.
If an increase is triggered, the U.S. trade representative office must allocate the additional quota within three days.
Despite adopting the formula, USDA retained the power to increase the quota if need be.
An increase might be necessary, the trade group said, because demand is expected to strength in summer and fall but flooding in the Red River Valley has slowed deliveries of beet sugar.
